🧭 Testicular Torsion

Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis. This summary reflects full-source review across Core Radiology GU pages 285-288 and Nucs page 485 plus the fused RadPrimer/STATdx master source.

📖 Summary
  • Testicular torsion is twisting of the testis and spermatic cord around the vascular pedicle, producing venous obstruction first and then arterial compromise, ischemia, and possible infarction.
  • It is a surgical emergency; viability depends on both symptom duration and degree of twist.
  • Classic presentation is acute scrotal or inguinal pain with swelling, abnormal lie, and an absent cremasteric reflex; younger children may present only with lower abdominal or groin pain.

🖼️ Key Imaging Findings
Ultrasound
  • Use a high-frequency linear transducer with grayscale plus color/power Doppler and compare both testes for size, echogenicity, lie, color flow, and waveforms.
  • Optimize low-flow detection with low pulse repetition frequency, low wall filter, and high Doppler gain.
  • The central clue is absent, decreased, or asymmetric intratesticular flow; early or partial torsion may have preserved flow and normal grayscale appearance.
  • The whirlpool sign is spiral or knot-like twisting of the spermatic cord cranial to the testis and is highly specific, especially when testicular flow is equivocal.
  • Delayed torsion produces enlargement and heterogeneous or mottled echotexture; testicular patching, fragmentation, hemorrhage, and necrosis predict nonviability.
  • Peripheral or paratesticular hyperemia may persist in missed torsion and must not be mistaken for viable intratesticular perfusion.
  • Partial/intermittent torsion may show normal, decreased, or absent flow during pain and hyperemia after detorsion; spectral Doppler may show diminished or absent diastolic flow.

Problem-solving modalities
  • CEUS: complete torsion lacks enhancement; partial torsion enhances more slowly or less than the opposite side.
  • MR may show decreased perfusion and a whirlpool pattern but should be reserved for rare equivocal cases and must not delay surgery.
  • Tc-99m pertechnetate scintigraphy may show reduced perfusion or focal photopenia/cold area with a dartos halo, but it is slower and has largely been replaced by ultrasound.

⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Torsion of the appendix testis/epididymis: blue-dot sign, hyperechoic appendage with central hypoechoic area, reactive hydrocele, and peripheral hyperemia.
  • Testicular infarction without cord torsion: absent flow but no whirlpool sign; may be segmental or global.
  • Epididymoorchitis/abscess: enlarged hyperemic epididymis/testis or a thick-walled focus with internal echoes; venous infarction can occasionally mimic torsion.
  • Trauma and tumor are additional mimics; rupture, hematocele, fracture plane, or focal abnormal vascularity may redirect the diagnosis.

⏱️ Board-Relevant Pivots
  • Doppler sensitivity in acute torsion is about 80-90%; a normal study does not exclude early, partial, or intermittent torsion.
  • Approximate salvage rates are 80-100% before 6 hours, 76% at 6-12 hours, 20% at 12-24 hours, and 0% after 24 hours.
  • Intravaginal torsion is the common pubertal type; extravaginal torsion is neonatal/perinatal.
  • Bell-clapper deformity reflects deficient posterior fixation and is often bilateral, explaining contralateral orchiopexy.
  • Treatment is immediate exploration, detorsion, and orchiopexy if viable; a nonviable testis is removed. Imaging must not delay management when clinical suspicion is high.

⭐ Super Summary
  • Acute pain + asymmetric/absent intratesticular flow or a cord whirlpool sign = torsion until proven otherwise; grayscale heterogeneity and patching signal delayed ischemic injury and poor viability.

column11: Why can early testicular torsion show absent Doppler flow with normal grayscale, while delayed torsion becomes enlarged and heterogeneous?
column12:
Normal substrate: The spermatic cord contains low-pressure venous outflow and arterial inflow to the testis.
Trigger: Cord twisting compresses veins first, producing congestion and edema, and then compromises arterial inflow.

Propagation: Persistent ischemia produces hemorrhage between lobules, necrotic islands, and tissue fragmentation.
Imaging result: The testis becomes enlarged, heterogeneous or mottled, with patching/fragmentation and absent flow; these delayed grayscale changes predict nonviability.

column11: Why does the spermatic cord form the whirlpool sign in testicular torsion?
column12:
Normal substrate: The spermatic cord is normally smooth and relatively linear as it carries vessels to the testis.
Trigger: Rotation of the testis winds the cord around its axis.

column11: How does bell-clapper deformity predispose to intravaginal testicular torsion?
column12:
Normal substrate: Posterior fixation by the tunica vaginalis/gubernacular attachment creates a testicular bare area that limits rotation.
Anatomic defect: Deficient posterior fixation leaves the testis more freely suspended within the tunica vaginalis.

column11: Why can a nonviable torsed testis show peripheral or paratesticular hyperemia?
column12:
Primary injury: The twisted cord eliminates or markedly reduces intratesticular perfusion.
Separate vascular compartments: The tunica, epididymal-cord complex, dartos fascia, and scrotal wall retain their own perfusion.
Reactive response: Ischemic injury and surrounding inflammation increase flow in these paratesticular tissues.
Imaging result: Color Doppler may show a bright peripheral rim despite absent true parenchymal flow.
Interpretive pivot: Peripheral flow is not evidence of testicular viability; verify that flow is genuinely intratesticular.

column11: What tissue injury explains testicular patching and fragmentation on ultrasound?

Vascular injury: Prolonged torsion causes venous congestion, hemorrhage, and arterial ischemia.
